title: Do Abiotic or Biotic Factors Influence Walleye Recruitment From Stocking in a Large Great Plains Reservoir?
content:
The relative influence of abiotic and biotic factors on walleye recruitment is evaluated in a large Great Plains reservoir. Recruitment is indexed from 30 years of annual survey data, and the influence of two abiotic and three biotic factors is assessed using an informationȁtheoretic modeling approach. Fingerling walleye stocking is identified as the primary driver of recruitment, while biotic factors explain more recruitment variability than abiotic factors.


ABSTRACT

Walleye (Sander vitreus) population densities have declined across their native and introduced ranges over the past few decades. These declines have often been linked to reduced recruitment, but most evaluations of recruitment have occurred on naturally recruiting populations. In this study, we examined abiotic and biotic factors influencing walleye recruitment in Lake McConaughy, Nebraska, which has been nearly annually stocked for 30 years. Walleye fingerlings have been stocked (∼35 mm total length) in Lake McConaughy since 1991, which primarily functions as an irrigation and hydropower reservoir. Recruitment was indexed using standardized fall experimental gill-net survey data from 1991 to 2020. Candidate models incorporated abiotic variables (total annual precipitation and winter severity) and biotic variables including stocking (total number of fingerlings stocked), predator abundance (combined catch per unit effort [CPUE] of white bass Morone chrysops, hybrid striped bass M. chrysops × Morone saxatilis and smallmouth bass Micropterus dolomieu) and competitor abundance (combined CPUE of alewife Alosa pseudoharengus and gizzard shad Dorosoma cepedianum). Models were compared using second-order Akaike's information criterion (AIC). Three top models were identified (∆AICc < 2.0). The best supported model included stocking and predator CPUE and explained 33% of annual recruitment variation. Stocking was included in all top models and had the highest relative variable importance (RVI), whereas predator CPUE had the second-highest RVI. Both variables were positively associated with walleye recruitment. Biotic variables explained a moderate portion of walleye recruitment variability and more strongly influenced recruitment compared to abiotic variables. Our results suggest that stocking is the primary driver of walleye recruitment in this system, necessitating refined management strategies given continued declines in adult walleye relative abundance. Future management efforts may benefit from considering how stocking strategies interact with system conditions such as predator abundance and prey availability to maximize survival of stocked fish.
